subject: chemistry_2

verification.note: Unit 10 (Noble Gases) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.89-90, the shaded sub-box "NOBLE GASES" of printed chapter 7; this question is printed on book p.89 as VSAQ 8. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. TWO BOOK ERRORS CORRECTED (book p.89, VSAQ 8). FIRST, the printed configuration is "(ns2 ns6)". There is no ns6 sub-shell; the filled octet is ns2 np6, and the card writes np6. SECOND, the printed answer says "Electron gain enthalpy is nearly zero". It is not near zero; it is large and POSITIVE for every noble gas (about +48 kJ/mol for He, +116 for Ne, +96 for Ar and Kr, +77 for Xe), which is why an electron is not taken up. The card writes large and positive. The rest of the printed answer, the filled octet, the exception of helium at 1s2, and the very high ionisation enthalpies, is correct and is kept. TREND AND EXCEPTION: the word "inert" in the question is itself an overstatement after 1962, so the card names xenon, krypton and radon as the elements that do form compounds.

steps.label: Completely filled valence shell
lines: Every noble gas has a completely filled

lines.text: Valence shell = ns² np⁶ (a filled octet)

lines: Helium is the exception. Its shell is 1s²,
which is also complete, because the first
steps.why: A filled shell means there is no partly filled orbital to share, lose or gain an electron with, so no ordinary bond can form. Helium has no p sub-shell at all in its only shell, so 1s² is a full shell for it even though it is not an octet.
common_mistakes: Writing the configuration as ns² ns⁶. There is no ns⁶ sub-shell; the filled octet is ns² np⁶.
Giving helium the same ns² np⁶ configuration. Helium is 1s² and has no p electrons.
steps.memory_tip: ns² np⁶ for all of them, and 1s² for helium alone.
steps.margin_note: Write the configuration in symbols and name helium as the exception. Both are needed for this mark.

steps.label: Ionisation and electron gain enthalpy
lines: Their ionisation enthalpies are the highest
in each period, so an electron is not lost.

lines.text: Electron gain enthalpy is large and positive

lines: so energy has to be supplied to add an
electron, and one is not gained either.
Exception: xenon, krypton and radon do form
steps.why: Neither losing an electron nor gaining one is possible. Losing an electron costs the most energy of any element in the period, and gaining one also costs energy rather than releasing it, because the added electron would have to start a new shell. The word inert is therefore an overstatement after 1962: xenon has the lowest ionisation enthalpy of the stable noble gases and reacts with fluorine and oxygen.
common_mistakes: Writing that the electron gain enthalpy is nearly zero or negative. It is large and positive for every noble gas.
Writing that no noble gas forms any compound. Xenon, krypton and radon do form compounds with fluorine and oxygen.
steps.memory_tip: Losing an electron costs too much energy, and gaining one also costs energy, so no bond forms.
steps.margin_note: Name both enthalpies. Naming only the high ionisation enthalpy usually reads as half this mark.

insider_note: Two reasons are needed, not one: the filled ns² np⁶ shell and the pair of enthalpies. Adding the line that xenon does form compounds shows the word "inert" has been read carefully and costs one line.
